en: Preface to the *Huayan jing jueyi lun* (Treatise on Resolving Doubts Concerning the Avataṃsaka Sūtra), composed by the Bhikṣu Zhàomíng of Mount Śītavana Monastery in the East.
Li Changzhe of Beijing was a scion of the imperial clan; his courtesy name was Tōngxuán. By nature, he was endowed with celestial acumen and wisdom.
Huiming was simple and unassuming; his learning did not rely on a single teacher, and his conduct was unfathomable.

He devoted himself to the Way of Ease, exhausting its subtle refinements to the utmost. He roamed freely among forests and springs, staying far from cities and towns; truly a "Prince's Son" (Wangsun) who had renounced his kingdom.

Having passed the age of forty, he ceased reading secular books; during the reign of Empress Wu Zetian, he devoted his heart to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and studied the commentaries of various ancient masters, sighing as he closed the volume:
"The text of this sūtra is vast and profound, and there are many schools of commentary."
Alas, those of later learning have no leisure to seek out the texts; how could they possibly engage in further practice?

Fortunately, I encountered the new translation of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, whose principles and meanings are perfectly complete. Consequently, I examined eighty fascicles of the scripture, extracted its subtle purports, elucidated its thematic gateways, and organized the sections from beginning to end, thereby completing the forty-fascicle *New Commentary on the Avataṃsaka*.

Fearing that the faculties of the people of his time were still shallow, he further composed the *Deciding Doubts* (*Jueyi lun*) in four fascicles, the *Brief Explanation* (*Lieshi*) in one fascicle, and the *Explanation of the Treatise on Dispelling Delusion, Revealing Wisdom, and Accomplishing Compassion through the Ten Clarities* (*Jiemixianzhichengbei shiming lun*) in one fascicle.

As for the *Ten Mysteries and Six Characteristics*, the *Ocean of Meaning in One Hundred Gates*, the *Practices of Samantabhadra*, the *Huayan Contemplation*, as well as various poems and prose compositions, all have been transmitted to the world.

Fearing that cold and heat might pass away and that the changes of the ages and shifts of custom would cause this to be lost, I have briefly recorded what I have seen and heard to transmit it to those who understand me.

It begins with his travels in the mountains of the East starting from the seventh year of the Kaiyuan era; he lived in seclusion and composed his treatises until his death on the twenty-eighth day of the third month in the eighteenth year of the Kaiyuan era.

At that time, at midnight, the mountain forest shook and resounded; flocks of birds cried out in confusion and hundreds of beasts fled in all directions. A white light issued from his crown and shot straight up toward heaven. Among those nearby, both monastics and laypeople, there was no one who did not lament and sigh in sorrow.
An observer remarked:
"Only Vimalakīrti and Samantabhadra of the Western Regions are of this lineage; Confucius and Laozi of this land do not belong to their category.
They are like the illusory manifestations of Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra."
Zhao Ming personally received his instructions and repeatedly attained the essence of his teachings.
Upon seeing his passing away, he sighed, lamenting that the Sage had left the world and that his aspirations could no longer reach him.

At that time, a gentleman who had come to seek the Way inquired of me regarding the origins and history of the former sage. Fearing that I might not speak of it, I have respectfully composed this preface.
Recorded on the eighth day of the seventh month of autumn in the Gengxu year of the Dali era.
